newsitem.title: SPAIN: Union, government fail to end Spain trucker strike.
newsitem.headline: Union, government fail to end Spain trucker strike.

text.p: The union leading a Spanish truckers strike failed to reach an agreement with the government in a first day of negotiations on Saturday to end the crippling stoppage.
The strike which has seriously disrupted commerce and cross-border traffic was to continue on Sunday when the union Fedatrans meets officials for another round of talks.
"We will be steadfast in the strike," Fedatrans spokesman Jose Luis Soldevilla told reporters.
Union representatives sat down with Development Ministry Director General of Transport Fernando Cascales in the afternoon for the first time in the 10-day-old strike.

Fedatrans had stayed away from negotiations between an inter-ministerial committee and transport associations, demanding the government meet with it separately. The government agreed to the separate talks late on Friday night.
The transport associations said on Saturday they had reached a preliminary accord with the government on truckers' demands for improved labour conditions and lower fuel prices.
They said they were in favour of ending the strike but added only Fedatrans could do so.
Fedatrans rejected the agreement and said it would not even be a basis for negotiations.

"Our desire is to call off the strike in the short term," Soldevilla said at a news conference. "But we will be very tough in the defence of the transporters' interests for which we are going to try to negotiate calmly without pressure."
Local news reports said the transport associations' preliminary accord included provisions for lowering diesel prices by five pesetas per litre and raising tariffs six percent.
The 10-day-old strike has caused major disruptions and been peppered with violence.
Fedatrans appealed to the strikers for calm on Saturday.
Like a French truckers strike last year which disrupted much of Western Europe with a 12-day blockade, Spanish drivers are demanding an overhaul of their sector.
They want their retirement age lowered to 60 from 65, recognition of professional illnesses and curbs on surging fuel prices among other demands.
Fedatrans said the main sticking point was early retirement.
The cabinet introduced deregulatory measures on Friday aimed at lowering fuel costs in a bid to appease strikers.
The union said the step was not enough.

The government warned on Friday the strike was causing grave damage to the Spanish economy and promised neighbours France and Portugal, the two countries most affected by the strike, it would ensure unimpeded movement on the roads.
The strike has choked roads in northern Spain, blocked ports and forced domestic and foreign carmakers to cut back or halt production at some factories.
Under government orders, security forces have been escorting trucks to ensure supplies of essential goods to areas where supplies had been cut off.
Thousands of striking trucks have lined up on the hard shoulders of main roads and pickets intimidated any drivers who dared to pass.
They have also blockaded border crossing with France and Portugal, trapping hundreds of foreign drivers at the frontiers.
